entities.name: Tammaritu
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Tammaritu II, a pivotal and ultimately tragic figure in the waning years of the Neo-Elamite kingdom, reigned as king of Elam in two brief, tumultuous periods: first from approximately 652 to 650 or 649 BCE, and again for a fleeting interlude in 648 BCE. As the son of Tammaritu I and successor to his uncle Ummanigash, Tammaritu II inherited a realm severely destabilized by internal dynastic struggles and the relentless imperial ambitions of the Neo-Assyrian Empire under Ashurbanipal. His reign encapsulates the desperate efforts of Elamite rulers to maintain independence against overwhelming Assyrian military and political pressure, ultimately culminating in the final destruction of Elam as a sovereign entity.

Tammaritu's initial ascent to the throne was marked by the ongoing Elamite involvement in the Babylonian revolt against Assyria, led by Ashurbanipal's brother, Shamash-shum-ukin. After the defeat and death of his predecessor Ummanigash, Tammaritu II continued the struggle, but faced a crushing defeat by Assyrian forces at the Battle of the Ulai River. This catastrophic loss forced him to flee to the coastal marshes and eventually surrender to Ashurbanipal in Nineveh. During his absence, Elam experienced further instability with the reigns of Indabibi and Humban-haltash III. Remarkably, Ashurbanipal briefly restored Tammaritu II to power in Susa in 648 BCE, likely as a puppet ruler, but this second reign was short-lived as internal Elamite factions and renewed Assyrian campaigns led to his final overthrow and the complete devastation of Susa by Assyrian armies.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Tammaritu II's reigns are historically significant because they mark the definitive end of the ancient Elamite kingdom as an independent power, leading directly to the destructive sack of Susa and the absorption of Elamite territories into the Assyrian Empire. His story exemplifies the final collapse of a major regional civilization under the pressure of imperial expansion.
